components.title: reference-web-server
components.description: A static HTTP server image on UBI 9 Micro, built to the container hardening standard.

control-implementations.description: Controls in the standard's baseline, as this image implements or hands them off.

implemented-requirements.remarks: Policy and procedures are written and maintained by the organization for the system. The standard is an input to them, not a substitute.

The image has no account of its own to manage: it ships no authentication configuration, no account store, and no management interface, and answers every request anonymously. The identity it runs as is the platform's: a numeric, non-root UID in group 0 (IMG-11), and any arbitrary UID the platform assigns (IMG-12). Account management for that identity is the platform's and the organization's, which the control baseline records as organization-inherited elsewhere. This answer belongs to a static file server: an image that verifies a token or session, holds a client secret, or decides authorization from claims takes part in identity, and these controls are image-owned or inherited from its identity provider, not inapplicable.
There is no account store to manage by automated means; see AC-2. The image adds none.

implemented-requirements.description: AC-2(2) Automated Temporary and Emergency Account Management.
implemented-requirements.remarks: There are no temporary or emergency accounts: the image issues no credentials of any kind; see AC-2.
There is no account to disable; see AC-2. The runtime identity is created and removed with the container, by the platform.
No account is created, modified, or removed in the image, so there is no such action to log; see AC-2. What the image does log is every request (AU-2).
The image holds no logon session to end on inactivity; HTTP requests are stateless and anonymous; see AC-2.
The image enforces no per-account usage conditions because it has no accounts; see AC-2. What may be requested, and from where, is the deployment's network policy (PLT-10).

implemented-requirements.description: AC-2(12) Account Monitoring for Atypical Usage.
implemented-requirements.remarks: There is no account whose usage could be atypical; see AC-2. Request-level monitoring is the platform's (PLT-16).

implemented-requirements.description: AC-2(13) Disable Accounts for High-risk Individuals.
implemented-requirements.remarks: An organizational process, performed for the system rather than by any component of it.

The image enforces what nginx enforces: it serves only files under the document root it ships, resolving each request with try_files and answering 404 otherwise, and it reads nothing outside that root. Which content exists, and who may reach it, is decided by what the deployment mounts and by its network policy (PLT-10); the image adds no access-control rules of its own.
Reached only by platform or host expectations.

implemented-requirements.description: AC-4(4) Flow Control of Encrypted Information.
implemented-requirements.remarks: Boundary protection is network policy at the platform (PLT-10). The image declares the flows it needs (IMG-30), which is what lets the policy be deny-by-default.
An organizational process, performed for the system rather than by any component of it.

Rests on IMG-11 Non-root, with no privilege transition; IMG-13 Works with no capabilities and no new privileges. The image cannot constrain what a deployment mounts or how it runs the image: the platform's part is PLT-02.

implemented-requirements.description: AC-6(1) Authorize Access to Security Functions.
implemented-requirements.remarks: The image separates no security functions by account because it has no accounts; see AC-2. It runs with every Linux capability dropped and no_new_privileges set, verified at runtime (IMG-13), so no process holds privilege to authorize.

implemented-requirements.description: AC-6(2) Non-privileged Access for Nonsecurity Functions.
implemented-requirements.remarks: Every process in the image runs as the same unprivileged, non-root identity; there is no privileged account to use for anything, security-related or not (IMG-11, IMG-13).

implemented-requirements.description: AC-6(3) Network Access to Privileged Commands.
implemented-requirements.remarks: The image exposes no privileged command, locally or over the network: it has no shell service, no administration endpoint, and no remote-administration daemon (IMG-27).
There is no privileged account to restrict: the image runs non-root with no capabilities, and carries neither su nor sudo, which the smoke suite verifies (IMG-09, IMG-11, IMG-13).
An organizational process, performed for the system rather than by any component of it.

implemented-requirements.description: AC-6(8) Privilege Levels for Code Execution.
implemented-requirements.remarks: Rests on IMG-09 No privilege-raising files; IMG-11 Non-root, with no privilege transition; IMG-12 Runs under an arbitrary UID; IMG-13 Works with no capabilities and no new privileges; IMG-31 Admitted under the restricted-v2 SCC and the Restricted Pod Security Standard; IMG-32 Runs in a user namespace under the restricted-v3 SCC. The image cannot constrain what a deployment mounts or how it runs the image: the platform's part is PLT-02.

implemented-requirements.description: AC-6(9) Log Use of Privileged Functions.
implemented-requirements.remarks: No privileged function executes in the image, so there is none to log; see AC-6(5). Every request it does serve is logged (AU-2, AU-12).

implemented-requirements.description: AC-6(10) Prohibit Non-privileged Users from Executing Privileged Functions.
implemented-requirements.remarks: Rests on IMG-11 Non-root, with no privilege transition; IMG-31 Admitted under the restricted-v2 SCC and the Restricted Pod Security Standard. The image cannot constrain what a deployment mounts or how it runs the image: the platform's part is PLT-02.
There is no logon to attempt, successfully or otherwise; the image authenticates nobody; see AC-2.
The image displays no system-use notification because it has no logon and no interactive session; see AC-2. Any banner in served content is the deployment's content.

The image controls no concurrent sessions by account, having none; see AC-2. Concurrent connections are bounded by worker_connections in the shipped configuration and by the deployment's resource limits (PLT-05).

There is no user session to terminate; each HTTP request is answered and closed, and idle connections end at nginx's keepalive timeout (SC-10); see AC-2.

implemented-requirements.description: AC-14 Permitted Actions Without Identification or Authentication.
implemented-requirements.remarks: The image serves its content without identification or authentication by design, which is what this control requires be documented and deliberate: it is a public, read-only HTTP server. Which content may be reached without authentication is the deployment's, through what it mounts and its network policy (PLT-10).
Remote access to the system is administration of the platform (PLT-13). The image offers no remote access of its own (IMG-27).

implemented-requirements.description: AC-17(2) Protection of Confidentiality and Integrity Using Encryption.
implemented-requirements.remarks: The image can protect remote access with TLS 1.2 or 1.3 when the deployment mounts a server block, certificate, and key read-only into /etc/nginx (IMG-16, IMG-17); the smoke suite proves it serves HTTPS that way. Whether remote access is encrypted in a given deployment is that deployment's decision, with the platform's (PLT-10).

nginx logs every request to standard output in its combined format, and every error to standard error at notice level, as the shipped nginx.conf sets. The image writes no log file, and the smoke suite reads a served request back out of the container's standard output (IMG-19).

Each access record carries the client address, the time, the request line, the status, the bytes sent, the referrer, and the user agent, which is nginx's combined format, the shipped default. Error records carry the time, severity, message, client, and request (IMG-19).

The image logs the combined format and adds nothing further. A deployment that needs more fields, such as a request identifier or upstream timing, mounts a server block setting its own log_format (IMG-16); the image neither prevents nor performs that.
The image writes its records to standard streams and keeps none. Storing, protecting, retaining, and processing them is the platform's log store (PLT-09).

The image ships one reviewed configuration file, owned by root and not writable by the runtime identity (IMG-10), with settings chosen for this standard: logs to the standard streams, server_tokens off, every writable path under the declared tmpfs, and listeners above 1024. What is not yet true is automated verification of those settings against a published benchmark; that waits on the SCAP profile (IMG-T3), which is why this control stays open.

implemented-requirements.description: CM-6(1) Automated Management, Application, and Verification.
implemented-requirements.remarks: As CM-6: the settings are fixed in the image and verified by the smoke suite in the properties they produce, but not yet by an automated check against a benchmark. The SCAP profile (IMG-T3) is the work that would close it.

The image identifies and authenticates no user: it has no logon, no session, and no credential store, and serves every request anonymously; see AC-2. Identifying the people who administer the platform is the platform's and the organization's. An image that validates a JWT, terminates mTLS, or keeps a session authenticates users, whoever issued the credential, and cannot answer this as this image does.

implemented-requirements.description: IA-2(1) Multi-factor Authentication to Privileged Accounts.
implemented-requirements.remarks: There is no privileged account, and so no multi-factor authentication for one; see IA-2 and AC-6(5).

implemented-requirements.description: IA-2(2) Multi-factor Authentication to Non-privileged Accounts.
implemented-requirements.remarks: There is no non-privileged account to authenticate, with one factor or several: the image serves every request anonymously and holds no credential store; see IA-2.

implemented-requirements.description: IA-2(5) Individual Authentication with Group Authentication.
implemented-requirements.remarks: The image uses no group authenticator, having no authentication at all; see IA-2.

implemented-requirements.description: IA-2(8) Access to Accounts — Replay Resistant.
implemented-requirements.remarks: There is no authentication exchange that could be replayed; see IA-2. Replay protection for the traffic itself comes from TLS when the deployment mounts it (SC-8, SC-23).
The image accepts no credentials at all, PIV included: it has no authentication path for a client to present one to; see IA-2.

The image manages no identifiers: it issues none, and the identity it runs as is assigned by the platform (IMG-11, IMG-12); see IA-2.
There is no identifier to mark as belonging to a contractor or a foreign national, because the image manages none; see IA-4.

The image manages no authenticators. It holds no password, key, or token of its own; the only secret it may be given is a TLS private key, which arrives as a read-only mounted file and is never written, logged, or placed in arguments or environment (IMG-16, ADR-0003).
No password authenticates anything in the image: it stores none, prompts for none, and has no account a password could belong to; see IA-5.

The image performs no public-key authentication of users. It does verify publisher signatures on its own inputs at build time, against a key pinned by full fingerprint (IMG-02), which is a different control (SI-7, CM-14).

The image protects the one authenticator it may be given, a TLS private key, as ADR-0003 requires: read-only, readable only by the container's user or a group it belongs to, never in arguments, environment, or logs. The smoke suite proves the key does not appear in any of them (IMG-16).
The image gives no authentication feedback because it authenticates nobody; see IA-2. It also discloses no version in its responses, since server_tokens is off (SI-11).

The image authenticates to no cryptographic module. It uses OpenSSL as Red Hat ships it, for TLS when a deployment mounts key material, and makes no FIPS claim; how this standard treats images that protect CUI is open (SC-13).
The image identifies and authenticates no non-organizational user, serving every request anonymously; see IA-2.

The image serves plain HTTP on 8080 as shipped, and TLS 1.2 or 1.3 on 8443 when the deployment mounts a server block, certificate, and key (IMG-16), which the smoke suite proves works. Whether transmission is protected in a given deployment therefore depends on that deployment, and on the platform's requirement that service traffic be encrypted (PLT-10, PLT-18).

The cryptography, when a deployment enables TLS, is OpenSSL as Red Hat ships it, restricted to TLS 1.2 and 1.3 by the server block the deployment mounts; the image ships no cipher policy of its own and makes no FIPS claim (SC-13, IA-7).

The shipped configuration sets no keepalive_timeout, so nginx's default applies and idle connections close without intervention; a deployment that needs a specific period sets it in a mounted server block (IMG-16). Disconnecting a session on organizational policy is the deployment's and the platform's.

TLS, when a deployment enables it, uses OpenSSL as Red Hat ships it in UBI 9, pinned in the lock by digest and signature (IMG-02). The image makes no FIPS 140-3 claim: this standard has not yet decided what it requires of images that protect CUI, which is why this control stays open rather than being answered here.

There are no spam-protection mechanisms to update, since the image handles no mail; see SI-8. The image's own inputs are kept current by a reviewed refresh (IMG-04, IMG-29).

nginx parses and rejects malformed requests, answering 400 rather than passing them on, and the image passes no input to an interpreter or application runtime because it hosts none. What is missing is a criterion and a check that prove the rejection, rather than relying on nginx's behaviour, which is why this control stays open.

The shipped configuration sets server_tokens off, so error responses carry neither the version nor build details, and errors go to standard error rather than to a client. What is missing is a criterion that requires error output be free of internal detail, and a check for it, which is why this control stays open.
